purpose: Acceptance length tau per model, drafter, workload and gamma, replacing assumed values. tau counts the target's bonus token, so tau is in [1, gamma+1]. Qwen3-8B points are MEASURED here; DeepSeek-V4-family points are CITED/DERIVED from published sources.

convention.tau: committed tokens per verification pass including the bonus token (DFlash eq. 1)
convention.survival_by_position: s_i = P(first i drafts all accepted); tau(gamma) = 1 + sum_{i<=gamma} s_i
convention.derived_tau_by_truncation: 1 + sum of the first g survival terms of a run at larger gamma. Grade 'derived': it is exact for a chain drafter only up to cycle re-alignment, and for a block drafter the shorter block is a different input, so it is not a run at that gamma.
convention.tau_mean: cycle-weighted: total committed tokens / total cycles over the workload
convention.tau_macro_mean_of_prompt_means: DFlash benchmark.py's own averaging: mean over prompts of per-prompt tau

throughput_c1.what: Absolute concurrency-1 decode rate of Qwen3-8B on the local GPU, greedy, batch 1, vLLM offline engine, prefix caching off. decode_tokens_per_s = sum(n-1) / sum(t_request - t_prefill), where t_prefill is a separate max_tokens=1 call on the same prompt; the whole-request rate (prefill included) is given too.
throughput_c1.caveat: The GPU is SHARED with other users' jobs; `contention` records, over each run's request windows, the device utilisation and the SM% and memory of every process that is not this measurement (nvidia-smi pmon, 10 s samples). Figures are a lower bound on an idle-GPU rate whenever other_sm_pct_max > 0.

sources.quote: Instead of predicting just the next single token, DeepSeek-V3 predicts the next 2 tokens through the MTP technique. ... Based on our evaluation, the acceptance rate of the second token prediction ranges between 85% and 90% across various generation topics, demonstrating consistent reliability. This high acceptance rate enables DeepSeek-V3 to achieve a significantly improved decoding speed, delivering 1.8 times TPS (Tokens Per Second).

Per-position acceptance decays fast: on DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 the last drafted token of a 7-token block survives less than 10% of the time, against more than 70% for the first. | DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, TP=8 on 8×B300 (SM100), expert parallel, FP8 KV cache, max_model_len 16384 ... The benchmark is 880 prompts at temperature 1.0, up to 2048 output tokens, swept over concurrency 1 to 256. | fixed k: "enable_adaptive_verification": false , "num_speculative_tokens": k , for k ≥ dspark_block_size (5 on this checkpoint) | --dataset-name speed_bench ... --speed-bench-dataset-subset qualitative
sources.workload: SPEED-Bench 'qualitative' subset, 880 prompts (240 at c=1), output cap 2048

sources.quote: For all benchmarks, we use standard speculative decoding ... with the sampling temperature set to 1.0. We report the accepted length (τ) per decoding round. ... all reported metrics for accepted length and acceptance rate include the target-generated bonus token. | Table 1: Qwen3-8B DSpark 6.17 5.78 5.01 5.16 5.52 5.17 3.72 3.58 3.21 | DSpark inherits the high initial acceptance of the deep parallel drafter (e.g., starting at 0.93 on Math). | We configure the maximum block size to γ = 5 and utilize the Markov head for sequential modeling. | expanding from MTP-1's static 2 tokens to roughly 4–6 tokens per request. | it consistently accelerates per-user generation speeds by 60%–85% (V4-Flash) and 57%–78% (V4-Pro) at matched aggregate throughput capacities.

sources.quote: We omit the MTP module during backbone pre-training and use DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026a) for speculative decoding. | The drafter comprises three Transformer blocks with a sliding attention window of 128 tokens. A single forward pass through these blocks computes base logits for five draft positions in parallel, while a lightweight Markov head models dependencies among the draft tokens. A confidence head predicts per-position conditional acceptance probabilities

gaps: Superseded 2026-09-28: V4.1-Flash-specific tau at the design gamma 5 now exists -- measured here (greedy, on-policy, 3.649 pooled, 95% CI [3.4995, 3.8412]) and published by third parties (vLLM PR #57432 GSM8K greedy 3.82-3.89 on the same revision; InferenceX T=1.0 coding 4.07 thinking-off / 3.51 thinking-on; production agentic thinking-on 3.43). DeepSeek itself still publishes no V4.1 acceptance figure (model card, tech report, API news).

No DeepSeek-V4 per-position acceptance table exists in any fetched source; the only DeepSeek-V4 per-position data are two endpoint bounds in the vLLM blog (pos 1 >70%, pos 7 <10%; V4-Pro-0813, T=1.0).

The DSpark paper publishes accepted length only for Qwen3-4B/8B/14B and Gemma4-12B targets (gamma=7, T=1.0); its DeepSeek-V4 section reports throughput/TPS gains and verify budgets (4-6 tokens), not tau.
The only published DeepSeek-V4 accept length is LMSYS '~5' (V4-Pro, B300, batch 1), with workload, gamma and temperature not stated.
LMSYS 5.24/3.78/2.91 (gsm8k/arena-hard/poetry, V4-Flash, block 6) are verify-window lengths, not accepted lengths.

No source reports acceptance on an agentic / tool-use workload. Workloads covered: 'various generation topics' (V3); SPEED-Bench qualitative (vLLM); gsm8k, arena-hard, poetry (LMSYS); GSM8K, MATH500, AIME25, MBPP, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench, MT-Bench, Alpaca, Arena-Hard on Qwen3/Gemma (DSpark paper); unlabelled live user traffic (DSpark paper, no tau). The paper names agent workloads only as motivation for per-request latency.

vLLM's V4-Pro-0813 is a later checkpoint than the V4-Pro/V4-Flash preview in the DSpark paper; its derived tau curve rests on a constant-rate interpolation between two bounds, so it is illustrative, not measured.

Sampling differs across sources: vLLM and DSpark offline use T=1.0 (probabilistic); HF cards' serving example uses draft_sample_method greedy; LMSYS frontier runs T=0.7; V3 unstated. Greedy acceptance is typically higher than T=1.0.
Served gamma differs: HF cards and vLLM use num_speculative_tokens 7 while dspark_block_size is 5 on V4-Pro-0813 and V4.1-Flash; DSpark paper production uses gamma=5; LMSYS mixed test uses block 6.
The DSpark paper's per-domain 'overall acceptance rate' at threshold 0 (Qwen3-4B: math 76.9%, code 67.6%, chat 45.7%) could not be reconciled with Table 1 tau under a simple definition; not used.

lossless_followup_mind2web.what: The one default-kernel vLLM divergence whose plain-run margin exceeded the 0.5-logit tie tolerance (agentic_mind2web, prompt 33964bc4-fc1d-417c-ba5a-2c1c45ed8d8b-step2, first difference at token 10, plain top-1/top-2 gap 2.0).
lossless_followup_mind2web.reruns: Re-run 2026-09-26 on the same engine: default kernels reproduce both outputs exactly (plain 67 tokens, DFlash 40 tokens, diverging at token 10 again); with VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 plain and DFlash are token-identical (88 tokens each). Token 4 of this prompt is itself a 0.0-logit tie under default kernels, and the batch-invariant run takes the other branch there.
lossless_followup_mind2web.verdict: Kernel-numerics divergence between a 16-position verification forward and a 1-position decode forward, not a verification bug: it vanishes with batch-invariant kernels, as do all 36 samples of the batch-invariant control run.

notes.throughput_c1_host_contention_note: The GPU sampler shows no other tenant's SM activity during any timed window, but the HOST was heavily loaded by other jobs (load average ~100-120 on 32 cores at the start of the session; not logged per window). DFlash at concurrency 1 is host/launch-bound far more than AR: the same BF16 DFlash c=1 measurement gave 270 tok/s on MATH-500 thinking-on at 15:57 (timing run) and 207 tok/s at 17:04 (energy run) with identical tau, while AR was 93-94 tok/s in both. Treat the timing run as the rate and the energy run's rate as a contended lower bound; energy per token is taken from the energy run (the only BF16 DFlash run with the 100 ms power log).
